steps.say: Some babies are born with an extra piece of lung that never connects to the airways. It sits apart from normal breathing tissue and drinks blood straight from the body's main artery instead of the lung circulation. Because it never ventilates, it becomes a home for repeated chest infections. It never helped with breathing and is found by accident or by infection.
steps.tx: **Sequestration** (detached lung piece) is nonfunctional dysplastic lung under **6** (six) percent of congenital lung anomalies, with no **tracheobronchial connection** (airway link) to the **tracheobronchial tree** (airway network) and a systemic **arterial supply** (body-artery feed) from the thoracic or infradiaphragmatic **aorta** (great body artery). It never contributed to breathing and is found by accident or **infection** (chest infection).

steps.say: The common variety hides inside the normal lung covering in the lower back corner of the chest. It drains through the lung veins and announces itself as pneumonia striking the same spot again and again. Two out of three cases sit in that posterior basal segment, clustering in one area. The whole lobe comes out when one segment cannot be separated safely.
steps.tx: **Intralobar sequestration** (shared-covering type) sits inside normal visceral **pleura** (lung wrapping) with pulmonary **venous drainage** (lung-vein return), makes two thirds (**2** (two) of **3** (three)) of cases in the **posterior basal** (lower back) segment, and presents with recurrent **pneumonia** (same-spot chest infection). Lobectomy follows when one **segment** (lung piece) cannot be separated safely.

vis.alt: Thoracic diagrams comparing arterial supply and venous drainage of intra- and extralobar sequestrations.
vis.caption: Intralobar versus extralobar supply and drainage patterns. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The rarer variety carries its own wrapping and drains to the body's veins instead. It tucks between the diaphragm and the lower lobe, sometimes hiding below it. It keeps company with hernias of the diaphragm, chest wall deformities and gut duplication cysts, complicating care.
steps.tx: **Extralobar sequestration** (own-covering type) has its own pleura with systemic **venous drainage** (body-vein return), hides between diaphragm and lower lobe or below the **diaphragm** (breathing sheet), and associates with diaphragmatic **hernia** (hole defect), **pectus** (sunken chest) and enteric **duplication cysts** (gut doubles). These are the classic **associated anomalies** (linked defects).

steps.say: Because no airway reaches this tissue, it never forms big air cysts and never bursts into the chest cavity. The dangers are different: it can bleed, become infected, twist on its own blood supply, or shunt so much blood that a newborn's heart fails from the extra load.
steps.tx: No airway connection means extralobar lesions never form big **cysts** (air pockets) or spontaneous **pneumothorax** (burst lung), but they can infarct, infect, bleed or twist, or shunt enough blood to cause high output **cardiac failure** (overloaded heart) and a **left to right shunt** (extra circuit) in neonates.

steps.say: Most of these lesions shrink away before birth as the growing body outruns their blood supply. The fetus is watched with repeated scans for fluid around the lung, excess amniotic fluid or whole-body swelling. Two thirds regress and never need an operation. Delivery is planned at a centre with children's surgeons on standby.
steps.tx: More than two thirds of prenatal lesions show **spontaneous regression** (natural shrinkage) as body growth outstrips **blood supply** (feeder flow), and fetuses are watched with serial **ultrasound** (sound-wave scans) for **pleural effusion** (lung-fluid collection), **polyhydramnios** (excess amniotic fluid) or **hydrops** (body swelling). Delivery planning includes a **paediatric surgical centre** (specialist unit) on standby.

steps.say: After birth a sound-wave scan with blood-flow colouring settles the anatomy. It shows whether the lump is solid or cystic and traces the rogue artery back to the aorta. Unclear or worrying scans move on to cross-sectional imaging for surgical planning. Contrast vessel scans map the feeder before any operation is booked.
steps.tx: Postnatal **Doppler ultrasound** (flow-tracing scan) defines cystic versus solid texture and maps the feeding systemic **artery** (rogue vessel), while **computed tomography** (detailed scan) or **magnetic resonance** (soft-tissue scan) is reserved for unclear or worrisome cases and operative mapping. Computed tomography **angiography** (vessel mapping) maps the feeder before any operation.

steps.say: Air inside one of these lumps is always abnormal. Since no airway connects to it, gas means a channel has opened to the gut. That single finding converts a routine resection into an operation that must find and close the fistula.
steps.tx: **Air** (gas) or **air fluid level** (gas-liquid line) inside an extralobar lesion is abnormal and suggests a **gastrointestinal fistula** (gut connection), since these lesions never communicate with the airway. Contrast or operative exploration then defines and closes the connection. Missed fistulas leak and infect.

steps.say: A mass sitting in the middle of the chest raises a different list of suspects. Each compartment of the mediastinum favours its own tumours and cysts, so placing the lesion front, middle or back narrows the diagnosis before any needle goes in. The compartment map guides that localisation.
steps.tx: **Mediastinal compartments** (chest zones) with characteristic masses aid diagnostic localisation: anterior lesions suggest germ cell or thymic disease, middle lesions vascular or nodal disease, and posterior lesions neurogenic tumours. Sequestration sits posteriorly, and compartment mapping separates it from foregut duplication and neurogenic masses.

vis.alt: Diagram of anterior, middle and posterior mediastinal compartments with characteristic masses.
vis.caption: Mediastinal compartments localise chest masses before biopsy. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Symptomatic or persistent lesions come out, and the operation follows the anatomy. Disease buried inside the lobe needs a segment or the whole lobe removed, while a separate lump lifts out on its own. Both approaches now travel through the keyhole camera whenever the child is stable. Follow-up pictures confirm the remaining lung has fully expanded.
steps.tx: Surgery is **segmentectomy** (segment removal) or **lobectomy** (lobe removal) for intralobar disease and **mass resection** (lump removal) for extralobar disease, done by open or **thoracoscopic** (keyhole chest) technique (**thoracoscopy** (camera surgery)). The feeding systemic artery is controlled first to prevent catastrophic bleeding. Postoperative imaging confirms full **expansion** (reinflation) of the remaining lung.
